audience: First-year physics students; no particle physics needed.
name: The Higgs hunt
notes: Working title. The 2011 LHC step rests on the ATLAS 2012 paper's introduction. The Tevatron step reports the CDF+D0 combination of July 2012 (arXiv:1207.6436), so it sits at 2012, after the LHC step, and selects Fermilab because the Tevatron and its experiments are not on the timeline after 2011. The first step has no `year`: its second sentence reports how the 2012 ATLAS paper described the Higgs boson, which was not true of 1990 (the top quark was still unobserved).

claims.covers: The mechanism that breaks electroweak symmetry in the Standard Model gives mass to massive elementary particles and implies the existence of a scalar particle, the Higgs boson
claims.quote: However, the mechanism that breaks electroweak symmetry in the SM has not been verified experimentally. This mechanism [5–10], which gives mass to massive elementary particles, implies the existence of a scalar particle, the SM Higgs boson.

claims.covers: In its discovery paper ATLAS described it as the only elementary particle in the Standard Model that had not yet been observed
claims.quote: The search for the Higgs boson, the only elementary particle in the SM that has not yet been observed, is one of the highlights of the Large Hadron Collider [11] (LHC) physics programme.

steps.text: The mechanism that breaks electroweak symmetry in the Standard Model gives mass to massive elementary particles and implies the existence of a scalar particle, the Higgs boson. In its discovery paper ATLAS described it as the only elementary particle in the Standard Model that had not yet been observed.
steps.title: Why a Higgs boson?

claims.covers: a collider with a 27 km circumference at CERN
reached a collision energy that topped 209 GeV in 2000
The four LEP collaborations, ALEPH, DELPHI, L3 and OPAL, collected 2461 pb⁻¹ of collision data at energies between 189 and 209 GeV and used it to search for the Standard Model Higgs boson
claims.quote: The four LEP collaborations, ALEPH, DELPHI, L3 and OPAL, have collected a total of 2461 pb-1 of e+e- collision data at centre-of-mass energies between 189 and 209 GeV. The data are used to search for the Standard Model Higgs boson.

steps.text: LEP, a collider with a 27 km circumference at CERN, reached a collision energy that topped 209 GeV in 2000. The four LEP collaborations, ALEPH, DELPHI, L3 and OPAL, collected 2461 pb⁻¹ of collision data at energies between 189 and 209 GeV and used it to search for the Standard Model Higgs boson.
steps.title: LEP searches at up to 209 GeV

claims.covers: the combined LEP search established a lower bound of 114.4 GeV/c² on the mass of the Standard Model Higgs boson, at the 95% confidence level
In June 2003
Indirect limits from precision electroweak measurements, as the LEP paper recalled, constrained the Standard Model Higgs boson mass to less than 193 GeV/c² at the 95% confidence level
claims.note: The paper is dated 13 March 2003 (CERN-EP/2003-011) and appeared on arXiv on 16 June 2003. The '...' stands for 'which depend logarithmically on the Higgs boson mass through radiative corrections. Currently these measurements predict that the Standard Model Higgs boson mass is mH = 81 (+52, -33) GeV/c2 and' (the superscripts and subscripts are garbled by text extraction); the omitted words run across a sentence boundary. The 158 GeV limit this step used before is the ATLAS 2012 paper's figure for the 2011 fits; it did not exist in 2003, so the step now quotes what the 2003 paper itself says.
claims.quote: indirect experimental limits are obtained from precision measurements of the electroweak parameters ... constrain its value to less than 193 GeV/c2 at the 95% confidence level

steps.text: In June 2003 the combined LEP search established a lower bound of 114.4 GeV/c² on the mass of the Standard Model Higgs boson, at the 95% confidence level. Indirect limits from precision electroweak measurements, as the LEP paper recalled, constrained the Standard Model Higgs boson mass to less than 193 GeV/c² at the 95% confidence level.
steps.title: No Higgs below 114.4 GeV

claims.covers: The LHC began high-energy collisions at 7 TeV on 30 March 2010
In their 2011 data ATLAS and CMS reported excesses compatible with SM Higgs boson production in the mass region 124–126 GeV, with significances of 2.9 and 3.1 standard deviations, respectively
claims.note: The sentence runs from the foot of the left column to the top of the right column on page 2 of the PDF; text extraction puts the page footer ('Preprint submitted to Physics Letters B') between 'standard' and 'deviations'. The '...' stands for 'of proton-proton (pp) collisions at centre-of-mass energy sqrt(s) = 7 TeV at the LHC,'. The quote is otherwise verbatim.
claims.quote: Both the ATLAS and CMS Collaborations reported excesses of events in their 2011 datasets ... which were compatible with SM Higgs boson production and decay in the mass region 124–126 GeV, with significances of 2.9 and 3.1 standard deviations (σ), respectively

steps.text: The LHC began high-energy collisions at 7 TeV on 30 March 2010. In their 2011 data ATLAS and CMS reported excesses compatible with SM Higgs boson production in the mass region 124–126 GeV, with significances of 2.9 and 3.1 standard deviations, respectively.
steps.title: The LHC and the first hints

claims.covers: The Tevatron at Fermilab collided protons and antiprotons at 1.96 TeV from 2002 through 2011 (Run II)
In July 2012
CDF and D0 combined their searches for a Higgs boson decaying to a bottom-antibottom quark pair
claims.quote: We combine searches by the CDF and D0 Collaborations for the associated production of a Higgs boson with a W or Z boson and subsequent decay of the Higgs boson to a bottom-antibottom quark pair.

claims.covers: reported evidence for a new particle, with a global significance of 3.1 standard deviations
claims.quote: The largest local significance is 3.3 standard deviations, corresponding to a global significance of 3.1 standard deviations. We interpret this as evidence for the presence of a new particle consistent with the standard model Higgs boson

steps.text: The Tevatron at Fermilab collided protons and antiprotons at 1.96 TeV from 2002 through 2011 (Run II). In July 2012 CDF and D0 combined their searches for a Higgs boson decaying to a bottom-antibottom quark pair and reported evidence for a new particle, with a global significance of 3.1 standard deviations.
steps.title: The Tevatron's evidence

claims.covers: On 4 July 2012 ATLAS and CMS presented their latest preliminary results in the search for the Higgs particle
ATLAS reported a neutral boson with a measured mass of 126.0 ± 0.4 (stat) ± 0.4 (sys) GeV
an observation with a local significance of 5.9 standard deviations

question.answer: The expected rate is one in 1 ÷ (1.7×10⁻⁹) ≈ 590 million, so about once in 590 million repetitions of the experiment.

claims.covers: a background fluctuation probability of 1.7×10⁻⁹

question.prompt: ATLAS quoted a background fluctuation probability of 1.7×10⁻⁹ for its excess. If there were no new particle, about how often would you expect a fluctuation this large at that mass?

steps.text: On 4 July 2012 ATLAS and CMS presented their latest preliminary results in the search for the Higgs particle. ATLAS reported a neutral boson with a measured mass of 126.0 ± 0.4 (stat) ± 0.4 (sys) GeV, in an observation with a local significance of 5.9 standard deviations.
steps.title: ATLAS's result

claims.covers: CMS observed an excess of events with a local significance of 5.0 standard deviations at a mass near 125 GeV, signalling the production of a new particle
A fit to the two decay modes with the best mass resolution gave a mass of 125.3 ± 0.4 (stat.) ± 0.5 (syst.) GeV

question.answer: Treating the uncertainties as independent and adding them in quadrature gives 0.57 GeV for ATLAS and 0.64 GeV for CMS. The masses differ by 126.0 − 125.3 = 0.7 GeV, with a combined uncertainty of √(0.57² + 0.64²) ≈ 0.85 GeV. That is 0.7 ÷ 0.85 ≈ 0.82 standard deviations, so the two measurements are consistent.
question.prompt: ATLAS measured the mass of the new particle as 126.0 ± 0.4 (stat.) ± 0.4 (sys.) GeV and CMS as 125.3 ± 0.4 (stat.) ± 0.5 (syst.) GeV. Do the two measurements agree?

steps.text: CMS observed an excess of events with a local significance of 5.0 standard deviations at a mass near 125 GeV, signalling the production of a new particle. A fit to the two decay modes with the best mass resolution gave a mass of 125.3 ± 0.4 (stat.) ± 0.5 (syst.) GeV.
steps.title: CMS's result

claims.covers: In June 2022
the ATLAS Collaboration reported that the Higgs boson discovered ten years ago is remarkably consistent with the predictions of the theory

steps.text: In June 2022 the ATLAS Collaboration reported that the Higgs boson discovered ten years ago is remarkably consistent with the predictions of the theory.
steps.title: Ten years on

summary: Follow the search for the Higgs boson from LEP, through the LHC's first hints and the Tevatron's evidence, to the announcement by ATLAS and CMS on 4 July 2012.
